title: A reverse translatase that writes a protein's sequence into nucleic acid

concept.text: Millennium Problems for Biology 3, The reverse translatase. Target: an enzyme that reads an untagged polypeptide and synthesizes a nucleic acid strand encoding its sequence, with no template or database lookup; for 100 or more random peptides of 50 or more residues, sequence accuracy at least 90%, average read length at least 25 residues and average quality at least Q10. Sources given: https://millenniumproblems.bio/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to BCH on 2026-11-15.
change_log.reason: One of the twelve Millennium Problems for Biology (Sam Rodriques and Michaela Hinks, FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, 2026), each with a stated concrete target; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: Reverse translatase
page.definition: A reverse translatase would be a purified protein or fixed protein complex that reads successive amino acids along an untagged peptide and writes their order into one nucleic acid strand. A code specified in advance assigns each amino acid a codon, a group of three nucleotides. Several natural codons can specify the same amino acid, so the peptide sequence alone cannot generally reveal the original gene sequence.

goal.need: Mass spectrometry often identifies peptides by matching fragments to a sequence database. Missing fragments can leave the amino-acid order ambiguous. In one benchmark, eight programs working without a database recovered a reference sequence for 64.2% of spectra even when a match by any program counted. A biologist could use an amplifiable record to read an unfamiliar peptide from a scarce sample on a DNA sequencer. That requires capturing the peptide and faithfully recording its residues. Copying the record cannot restore a missing residue.

statements.quote: Each problem is intended to be very difficult to solve, but easy to validate in a simple laboratory environment.
statements.context: Their 12-problem research agenda, announced on 23 September 2026, includes the reverse translatase as Problem 3.

statements.quote: Create an enzyme that can “reverse translate” an arbitrary peptide sequence into RNA or DNA.
statements.context: Problem 03, The reverse translatase, in The Millennium Problems for Biology.

completion.title: An enzyme passes the reverse-translatase challenge on at least 100 pooled random peptides.
completion.criterion: A purified protein catalyst or fixed protein complex processively converts untagged polypeptides into covalent nucleic acid under a preregistered codon convention. Pool ≥100 preregistered, synthesized random peptides, each ≥50 residues: sequence accuracy ≥90%; mean read length ≥25 residues; mean quality should be ≥Q10. Exclude nucleic-acid templates, preattached sequence barcodes, residue-specific operator cycles and dictionary/database lookup. Output must support ordinary polymerases and ligases, and downstream amplification or sequencing.
completion.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, Millennium Problems for Biology, Problem 03.
completion.basis: This is the challenge's published test. The precursor experiments use RNA catalysts or operator-controlled chemical cycles.

milestones.title: Glutamine and arginine trigger release of their RNA codons with more than 50% self-cleavage.
milestones.criterion: Two RNA catalyst designs release CAG in response to glutamine and CGG in response to arginine, reaching >50% self-cleavage within 45 minutes and 8 hours, respectively, with magnesium present. Shi et al. reported these component results on 26 February 2026. They demonstrated the proposed reactions separately; their system did not processively copy peptide sequences.
milestones.set_by: Shi et al., published experimental protocol, Figures 2C and 2E. These are study-specific component tests using RNA catalysts, not a field-wide reverse-translatase benchmark.

milestones.title: DNA reporters identify four residues at their positions in five cycles on a bulk peptide sample.
milestones.criterion: Run five chemical sequencing cycles on approximately 100 pmol of the model peptide RGFDWGX. Use the cycle and antibody barcodes to identify arginine at position 1, phenylalanine at 3, aspartate at 4 and tryptophan at 5. Glycine at position 2 serves as the background control because the assay uses no glycine-specific antibody.
milestones.set_by: Zheng et al., 2024 preprint Figure 5B and 2026 Nature Biotechnology Figure 4b, ensemble sequencing assay.
milestones.threshold_quote: We performed five cycles of sequencing on ~100 pmol peptide.

milestones.title: An enzyme copies at least 100 random peptides of at least 50 residues each in separate reactions.
milestones.criterion: Meet the completion test in separate reactions: ≥100 preregistered random peptides, each ≥50 residues; ≥90% accuracy; mean read length ≥25 residues; mean quality should be ≥Q10. Retain its catalytic, coding and output-compatibility conditions. Pooling remains untested.
milestones.set_by: Atlas proposal. Searches of the Millennium Problems, DARPA PROSE documents and peptide-to-DNA papers found no externally specified enzyme intermediate. This proposal retains the completion assay with pooling removed.

milestones.title: An engineered RNA transfers one AGG codon to an eight-nucleotide RNA.
milestones.criterion: Ligate the 83-nucleotide donor RNA to the eight-nucleotide acceptor RNA and resolve the products after self-cleavage. The acceptor must gain the AGG triplet to give an 11-nucleotide product, with a corresponding 80-nucleotide donor product.

milestones.title: Glutamine triggers CAG release with more than 50% RNA self-cleavage within 45 minutes.
milestones.criterion: Test the type 2 glutamine-responsive RNA at 50 °C with 50 mM free glutamine and 0.5 mM magnesium chloride. Require release of CAG and greater than 50% self-cleavage by 45 minutes. Compare with controls lacking glutamine or magnesium.
milestones.set_by: Shi et al., Figure 2C glutamine-response assay.

milestones.title: Arginine triggers CGG release with more than 50% RNA self-cleavage within eight hours.
milestones.criterion: Test the type 2 arginine-responsive RNA at 12 °C with 50 mM free arginine and 0.5 mM magnesium chloride. Require release of CGG and greater than 50% self-cleavage by eight hours. Compare with controls lacking arginine or magnesium.
milestones.set_by: Shi et al., Figure 2E arginine-response assay.

milestones.title: DNA reporters recover all four tested positions on an individual peptide molecule.
milestones.criterion: Apply four chemical sequencing cycles to 0.5 fmol of the peptide of interest in the presence of 100 pmol of carrier peptide. Group DNA reporters by the unique molecular identifier assigned to the source molecule. A complete read must identify the correct residue at each of the four positions within one group. Report missing positions separately from incorrect calls.
milestones.set_by: Zheng et al., Nature Biotechnology Figure 5, single-molecule peptide sequencing assay.
milestones.threshold_quote: achieving full sequence coverage in millions of reads

not_found: No externally specified intermediate performance benchmark for a purified reverse-translatase protein catalyst was found.
No published result satisfying the challenge's protein-catalyst and pooled-peptide conditions was found.
The challenge does not define the sequence-accuracy denominator, random-peptide sampling distribution or Q-score calculation.
The full text of the 2026 Nature Biotechnology paper on single-molecule peptide-to-DNA sequencing could not be opened.
No academy, professional society or programme statement disputing the feasibility or value of the specified enzyme challenge was found.
